```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)
library(patchwork)

penguins2 <- penguins |>
  select(species, bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm) |>
  drop_na()

overall_mod <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm, data = penguins2)
species_mod <- lm(bill_depth_mm ~ bill_length_mm + species, data = penguins2)
# Signed, fixed-precision so the two halves of the headline stat are
# typographically parallel (e.g. "-0.09 -> +0.20", not "-0.09 -> +0.2").
overall_slope <- sprintf("%+.2f", coef(overall_mod)[["bill_length_mm"]])
species_slope <- sprintf("%+.2f", coef(species_mod)[["bill_length_mm"]])
overall_r <- cor(penguins2$bill_length_mm, penguins2$bill_depth_mm)
by_species_r <- penguins2 |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarize(r = cor(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm), n = n())

p_pooled <- ggplot(penguins2, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, color = "#666666", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              color = "#A8384F", linewidth = 1.1) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       title = "All species pooled") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15)

p_species <- ggplot(penguins2, aes(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("#0047B3", "#CC0033", "#00205B")) +
  labs(x = "Bill length (mm)", y = "Bill depth (mm)",
       title = "Same data, by species", color = "Species") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 15) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

# Rendered once here so both the HTML and print figures draw from the
# same objects.
evidence_plot <- p_pooled | p_species
```

## The Headline Finding

Slope of bill depth on bill length (mm per mm): pooling every species together gives **`r overall_slope`**, but adding species to the model as a covariate reverses it to **`r species_slope`**. In other words, bill depth *falls* as bill length rises when every species is lumped together, but *rises* with bill length once each species is considered on its own -- a textbook **Simpson's paradox**.

## Why It Matters

- A pooled regression can hide -- or completely invert -- the pattern that actually holds within each group. Here the sign flips from negative to positive once species enters the model.
- Whenever a natural grouping variable (species, site, cohort) is available, check whether it changes the story before trusting an aggregate result -- a pooled effect is a starting point, not a conclusion.
- Simpson's paradox is common wherever subgroups differ in both their typical predictor value and their typical outcome, e.g. comparing outcomes across hospitals, schools, or -- as here -- species with systematically different bill sizes.

## How We Studied It

- **Data:** `palmerpenguins` [@horst2020palmerpenguins], collected at Palmer Station, Antarctica [@gorman2014ecological]; `r nrow(penguins2)` penguins with complete bill measurements across three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo).
- **Models:** compared a pooled regression of bill depth on bill length to one that adds species as a covariate, so each species gets its own intercept but a shared slope.
- **Direct check:** also computed the bill length/bill depth correlation *within* each species separately (@tbl-by-species-cards) to confirm the reversal isn't an artifact of the linear model form.
- Built in R [@rcore2026] with the tidyverse [@tidyverse2019], ggplot2 [@ggplot22016], and patchwork [@patchwork2025] for the side-by-side figure at right.

## Ethics & Broader Impact

::: {.ethics-panel}
**Generative AI use.** Portions of this poster's R code and prose were drafted with the assistance of an AI coding assistant (Claude, via Posit's Positron/Assistant integration) for code scaffolding, prose editing, and citation formatting. The human author(s) reviewed and verified every analysis, figure, and conclusion and remain fully accountable for the content. No generative AI was used to fabricate, alter, or synthesize the underlying penguin measurement data, which are used unmodified from the published `palmerpenguins` dataset.

**Privacy & data governance.** This analysis uses only publicly available, non-human biometric measurements of penguins; it contains no personally identifiable information, so no de-identification, IRB review, or GDPR/EU AI Act data-protection provisions apply. The original field data were collected under the data providers' own institutional and permitting approvals.

**Bias, fairness & broader impact.** This is a descriptive/inferential statistics example, not a deployed predictive or classification system, so no demographic-fairness audit or dual-use/weaponization risk assessment applies. Computational cost is negligible: fitting two linear regressions on 342 rows completes in milliseconds on a laptop, with no large-model training and no meaningful carbon footprint.
:::

## Evidence

```{r}
#| label: fig-simpson-before-after
#| fig-cap: "Pooling across species (left) suggests bill depth decreases with bill length. Looking within each species (right) shows the opposite: bill depth increases with bill length in every species."
#| echo: false
#| out-width: "20in"
#| fig-width: 14
#| fig-height: 6.5
evidence_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-by-species-cards
#| tbl-cap: "Within-species correlation between bill length and bill depth is positive for all three species."
#| echo: false
by_species_r |>
  mutate(r = round(r, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Species", "Correlation (r)", "n"))
```

## What's Next

- Test whether the within-species slope itself differs by species (a length &times; species interaction), and whether sex explains any of the remaining within-species scatter.
- Add sex and island as further covariates -- both are recorded in `palmerpenguins` but unused here.
- Extend the same pooled-vs-adjusted comparison to flipper length and body mass, to see whether the same reversal shows up elsewhere in the dataset.
